passage.title: Bigfoot
lines: Bigfoot is a humanlike creature reportedly living in the Pacific Northwest. Sightings of it
have been noted most often in the mountainous areas of Northern California, Oregon, and
Washington in the United States. It has also been seen many times in British
Columbia in Canada, where it is called Sasquatch.
Witnesses describe a creature that is tall by human standards, measuring 7 to 10 feet (2 to 3
meters). It looks like an ape, with thick, powerful, fur-covered arms and a short, strong
neck; however, the way it walks upright is more like that of Homo sapiens.
Although hundreds of sightings of Bigfoot have been reported, most experts have not seen
enough evidence to be convinced that it exists. The fact that some alleged evidence has been
proven fake may have discredited other, more credible information.

passage.title: Epinephrine
lines: The next hormone is epinephrine, also called adrenaline. This hormone is a natural secretion of the
adrenal glands in the human body. Its main function is to help the body cope
with sudden surges of stress. When a person unexpectedly finds himself in a stressful situation
filled with fear or anger, a large amount of epinephrine is released into the blood and the body
responds with an increased heartbeat, higher blood pressure, and conversion of glycogen into glucose
for energy so the body can deal with the stress.
Epinephrine can be extracted from the adrenal glands of animals or synthesized
chemically so that it can be put to further use. It is used in the treatment of severe asthma, where it
relaxes the large muscles of the bronchi, the large air passages leading into the lungs. It is also used in
cases of severe allergic reaction or cardiac arrest.

passage.title: The banking crisis of 1933
lines: A massive banking crisis struck the United States in 1933. In the two preceding years, a
large number of banks had failed, and fear of lost savings had led many depositors to withdraw
their funds. Problems became so serious in Michigan that Governor William
A. Comstock was forced to declare a moratorium on all banking activities in the state on February 14,
1933. The panic quickly spread to other states, and on March 6, President Franklin D.
Roosevelt declared a banking moratorium across the United States, leaving the entire country
without banking services.
Congress met immediately in a special session to solve the crisis and on March 9
passed the Emergency Banking Act of 1933 to help financially healthy banks reopen. By March
15, banks controlling 90 percent of the country's financial reserves were open for business again.
